analysis.one_liner: Ends tax-credit landlords' early exit from 30-year low-rent commitments after 15 years.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have preserved affordable rents at expiring low-income housing tax credit properties, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in June 2019 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal low-income housing tax credits pay developers to build apartments with below-market rents. Under the qualified contract option, owners can ask the state after year 15 to buy them out of the deal and convert the building to market-rate rents — years before the 30-year affordability commitment ends. This bill would repeal that option for nearly all existing buildings and require owners who leave early to sell at a price that reflects the rent restrictions, keeping those apartments affordable for the full 30 years.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income tenants living in apartments financed with low-income housing tax credits, especially those in buildings old enough to be eligible for the year-15 conversion. They keep their rents at below-market levels for the full 30-year affordability period instead of facing conversion to market rates. State housing credit agencies also gain a clearer hand in enforcing affordability.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the qualified contract option for buildings that received their tax credit allocation before January 1, 2019, so owners can no longer convert to market-rate rents after 15 years.

Requires owners who sell an existing building to sell both the market-rate and low-income portions at a fair market value that accounts for the rent restrictions, ensuring the property keeps meeting affordability standards.
Under current law, the qualified contract option lets property owners convert to market rate after 15 years even though properties are subject to a 30-year affordability period at below-market rents.

analysis.who_pays: Owners of tax-credit buildings and the investors who bought tax credits expecting to sell or reposition the property at year 15 lose the right to convert it to market-rate rents, which reduces the resale value of the property and the value of their investment. Congress would forgo none of the credit directly, but the change would make tax-credit equity somewhat less attractive to future investors.

drawbacks.text: The change reduces the value of existing tax-credit investments, since a building worth market rates after year 15 is worth less if its rents are locked in for 30 years; investors and affordable-housing advocates have long argued over how much this burden should fall on existing deals rather than only new ones.

Repealing the option does not by itself add a single new affordable apartment; it only preserves the stock that already exists, and if it deters future investment in tax-credit housing it could slightly slow construction of new affordable units.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete: thousands of apartments that would otherwise convert to market rents after 15 years stay affordable for the full 30-year commitment, at no new cost to taxpayers. The cost falls on private owners and investors who priced the year-15 exit into their deals, which is a real but one-time fairness grievance rather than a public loss. The bill is narrowly drafted and does not address the larger shortage of affordable housing; it protects what exists instead of building more.

outcome.mechanism: Wyden introduced it in June 2019 and the Senate sent it to the Finance Committee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Wyden, joined by Sens. Young, Cardin, and Brown, introduced the bill on June 25, 2019 to repeal the qualified contract option in the low-income housing tax credit rules.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day; no further action was ever taken on it.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2021 with the bill still in committee, so it received no hearing, markup, or floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners of tax-credit buildings and their investors, who keep the right to convert properties to market rents after 15 years, and the tax-credit equity market that prices that option in.

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.role: Senate Finance Committee ranking member; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Save Affordable Housing Act to repeal the qualified contract option and preserve 30-year affordability at existing tax-credit buildings.

for.name: Sen. Todd Young
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it bipartisan at introduction.

for.name: Sens. Sherrod Brown and Ben Cardin
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors alongside Wyden.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred to his committee; it stayed there until Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start — five Democratic and one Republican cosponsors on a bill from the Finance Committee's top Democrat — but the committee never took the bill up, so no votes exist to measure the parties' positions.

industries.industry: Low-income housing tax credit investors and syndicators
industries.note: The bill removes the year-15 qualified contract exit, which cuts the resale value of existing tax-credit investments because a building with locked-in low rents is worth less than one free to charge market rates. The industry's financial interest in this bill runs directly against tenants who would face market-rent conversion.

industries.industry: Owners of existing tax-credit apartment buildings
industries.note: Owners who counted on converting buildings to market rate after 15 years would have to honor the full 30-year affordability commitment instead, or sell at a price that accounts for the rent restrictions.
The bill gives agencies the job of setting the restricted fair-market price at sale and enforcing continued affordability, expanding their oversight role without adding dedicated funding.
